new_statements.rule_in_words: The source characterises Salka Kambari (Tsishingini) as a two-level-tone language with light lexical tone load and a Salka-specific ban on word-initial High tone (nouns L-initial; imperative verbs mostly LH); it gives NO statement about the existence or location of word stress. The only occurrence of 'stress' in the book is an appendix heading 'Unstressed /u/' (p. 200, Auna Kambari/Tsikimba) describing a reduced root-final vowel before suffixes, which is not a stress-placement rule and not about the Salka variety.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone only: imperative verbs 'nearly always LH' with some LL exceptions (e.g. zama 'search'); no HH nouns; Salka lacks the H-initial noun patterns found in Auna/Agwara.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone patterns given for citation forms elicited in isolation (nouns with class prefix; verbs in the imperative); grammatical tone on verbs said to be redundant with subject-pronoun set. Phonology chapter treats the three Kambari co-languages together, flagging Salka-specific facts.
new_statements.identity_note: Naming trap: Crozier (1984, 1993) uses 'Cishingini'/'Kambari' for Central (Salka) Kambari = Glottolog tsis1238 / ISO tsw, whereas Stark (2004, 2010) uses 'Cishingini' for Agwara (Western) Kambari = cish1238 / asg and 'Tsishingini' for Salka (Blench & McGill 2012:9 make the same point; SIL archive files Crozier 1984 under tsw). Stark 2010 describes the three co-languages jointly (examples mostly Auna Kambari = Tsikimba, tsik1238) and flags Salka-specific facts, notably the ban on word-initial High tone; the 'Unstressed /u/' note (p. 200) is in the Auna Kambari (Tsikimba) orthography appendix, not Salka. Hoffmann 1965's 'Central Kambari' is Raba and Salka speech (tsw). The Rosetta extract of Alphabets of Africa is filed under asg but per Stark 2010:1.6.1 reflects Crozier's Salka-based work.
